pillars.title: Human Psychology & Buyer Behaviour
pillars.description: The complete map of cognitive biases and emotional triggers that drive purchasing decisions.

concepts.name: Loss Aversion
concepts.definition: People feel the pain of losing something roughly twice as intensely as the pleasure of gaining the equivalent. Losses loom larger than gains.
concepts.business_application: Frame offers as 'Don't miss out' rather than 'Gain this'. Highlight what the customer loses by NOT buying.

concepts.name: Anchoring Effect
concepts.definition: The first number a person sees becomes the psychological reference point for all subsequent judgments of value.
concepts.business_application: Always show a higher 'original price' before the sale price. Lead with your premium tier in pricing tables.

concepts.name: Social Proof
concepts.definition: Humans look to others' behaviour to determine the correct action, especially in uncertain situations.
concepts.business_application: Show real-time purchase counts, review counts, customer logos, and testimonials prominently.

concepts.name: Scarcity Trigger
concepts.definition: Items perceived as scarce are valued more highly than identical items that are abundant.
concepts.business_application: Communicate genuine stock limits, seat limits, or time windows. Even perceived scarcity changes conversion rates.

concepts.name: Decision Fatigue
concepts.definition: The quality of decisions deteriorates after a long session of decision making. Too many choices leads to no choice.
concepts.business_application: Reduce options. Highlight a 'Most Popular' plan. Use a clear recommended path through your product.

concepts.name: IKEA Effect
concepts.definition: People place disproportionately high value on products they have partially created or customised themselves.
concepts.business_application: Allow customers to personalise, configure, or co-create. Involve them in the product.

concepts.name: Endowment Effect
concepts.definition: People value something more once they feel they own it, even temporarily.
concepts.business_application: Free trials with full access create ownership feeling. 'Your personalised dashboard' language increases attachment.

concepts.name: Reciprocity
concepts.definition: When someone gives us something, we feel a psychological obligation to give something back.
concepts.business_application: Lead with genuine free value — guides, audits, tools — before asking for the sale.

concepts.name: Foot-in-the-Door
concepts.definition: Agreeing to a small request increases likelihood of agreeing to a larger request later.
concepts.business_application: Get micro-commitments first: email signup → free trial → paid plan. Each yes makes the next yes easier.

concepts.name: Decoy Effect
concepts.definition: Introducing a third, clearly inferior option makes one of the original options look significantly more attractive.
concepts.business_application: Design your pricing tiers so the middle option looks like the clear winner. The decoy makes the target irresistible.

pillars.title: Market Structure Analysis
pillars.description: Frameworks to understand the forces, dynamics, and topology of any market your business operates in.

concepts.name: Porter's Five Forces
concepts.definition: A framework that identifies five competitive forces that shape every industry and market.

forces.name: Threat of New Entrants
questions: How easy is it to enter your market?

forces.name: Threat of Substitutes
questions: What else solves your customer's problem?

forces.name: Competitive Rivalry
questions: Is the market growing or shrinking?

concepts.name: Blue Ocean Strategy
concepts.definition: Creating uncontested market space by making competition irrelevant, rather than competing in existing (red) oceans.
concepts.business_application: Identify factors the industry competes on, eliminate or reduce the ones customers don't value, raise or create factors they do.
tools: Four Actions Framework (Eliminate, Reduce, Raise, Create)

concepts.name: Market Saturation Detection
concepts.definition: Understanding whether a market is approaching its maximum penetration level, signaling declining margins and intense competition.

concepts.name: Demand Elasticity Modeling
concepts.definition: Price elasticity measures how sensitive demand is to price changes. Elastic demand drops sharply with price increases; inelastic demand holds.
concepts.business_application: Know whether you can raise prices without losing volume. Luxury goods are inelastic; commodities are elastic.
concepts.formula: Elasticity = % Change in Quantity / % Change in Price
tactics: Test small price increases on a segment
Monitor competitor price changes and your volume response

pillars.title: Money Flow Intelligence
pillars.description: Understanding where capital moves, how revenue should be structured, and how cash timing affects business survival.

types.description: One-time product or service sales. High acquisition cost, no guaranteed repeat.
Predictable monthly or annual revenue. Most valuable for valuation multiples.
Customers pay for what they consume. Lower barrier to entry, volatile revenue.
IP, brand, or technology rented to others. Highly scalable, minimal marginal cost.
Take rate on transactions between two sides. Network effects compound value.
Free tier creates user base; conversion to paid monetises the top percentage.

concepts.name: High-Margin vs High-Volume Tradeoff
concepts.definition: Two fundamentally different profit strategies: few customers paying a lot, or many customers paying a little.
concepts.danger_zone: Trapped in middle — not cheap enough to win on volume, not premium enough to justify high price.

concepts.name: Cash Flow Timing Intelligence
concepts.definition: A profitable business can still die from cash flow problems if money exits before it enters.
tactics: Build a 3-month cash reserve before scaling spend
warning_signs: Paying suppliers before collecting from customers

concepts.name: CAC vs LTV Framework
concepts.definition: Customer Acquisition Cost vs Lifetime Value. The ratio determines whether your business model is fundamentally profitable.
concepts.healthy_ratio: LTV should be at least 3x CAC for a sustainable business.

pillars.title: Price Pattern Recognition
pillars.description: The science and psychology of pricing — how to set, communicate, and change prices to maximise revenue and perceived value.

concepts.name: Psychological Price Thresholds
concepts.definition: Prices just below round numbers (₹99, ₹999, ₹4,999) feel significantly cheaper than the round number above.
concepts.explanation: Buyers read left-to-right, so ₹999 registers as '9 hundred' before processing the full number. The first digit dominates perception.
concepts.application: Always price below the threshold unless you are signalling premium. ₹10,000 can signal quality where ₹9,999 looks cheap.

concepts.name: Value-Based Pricing
concepts.definition: Setting price based on what the customer perceives the outcome is worth, not based on cost-plus logic.
concepts.business_application: If your product saves a customer ₹50,000 per year, pricing at ₹12,000 per year is defensible regardless of your cost.
steps: Identify the specific outcome the customer achieves
Quantify that outcome in money or time
Price at 20-30% of the value delivered

concepts.name: Penetration Pricing Strategy
concepts.definition: Entering a market with a low price to capture market share quickly, with the intention to raise price later.
risks: Trains customers to expect low prices
Attracts price-sensitive customers who churn when price rises
when_to_use: Network-effect businesses where scale matters more than early margin

concepts.name: Premium Pricing Signals
concepts.definition: Counterintuitively, a higher price often increases perceived quality and desirability.
conditions: Product quality is hard to evaluate before purchase
Competitors cluster at lower prices creating a gap
execution: Invest in premium packaging and presentation
Be selective about who you sell to

concepts.name: Discount Timing Intelligence
concepts.definition: When and how you discount matters as much as how much you discount.
rules: Never discount without a reason (undermines price integrity)
Seasonal discounts maintain integrity better than random ones
Bundle discounts preserve individual product price perception
Loyalty discounts reward behaviour without training all customers to wait for sales
dangerous_patterns: Training your audience to never pay full price

pillars.title: Competitive Battlefield Analysis
pillars.description: Systematic frameworks for understanding, monitoring, and outmanoeuvring competitors.

concepts.name: Competitor Weakness Mapping
concepts.definition: Systematically identifying the gaps, vulnerabilities, and underserved customers of each competitor.
dimensions: Review sentiment analysis (what customers complain about)
concepts.method: For each competitor, read their 1-star and 2-star reviews. The complaints are a direct map of opportunities.

concepts.name: SWOT Live Analysis
concepts.definition: A dynamic Strengths-Weaknesses-Opportunities-Threats framework tied to specific actions, not just a static matrix.

action_mapping.SO_strategy: Use strengths to capitalise on opportunities

concepts.name: Counter-Move Playbook
concepts.definition: Pre-planned strategic responses to the most likely moves competitors will make.

options: Do not match — differentiate on value
Bundle to change the price comparison
Reposition your product against their weakness
Acquire or partner with a complementary player
Target their brand keywords with comparison ads
Double down on community and organic
Launch a PR story about a different angle

concepts.name: First-Mover vs Fast-Follower
concepts.definition: Being first in a market carries brand recognition advantages but also the cost of educating the market. Fast followers learn from first-mover mistakes.
fast_follower_advantages: Enter when the market is proven
Compete on execution rather than education
concepts.recommendation: In technology markets, fast-follower with superior execution often wins. In brand-driven markets, first-mover advantage is more durable.

pillars.title: Winning Business Strategies
pillars.description: Proven playbooks for growth, retention, scaling, and building durable competitive advantages.

concepts.name: Growth Hacking Frameworks
concepts.definition: High-velocity, low-cost experiments designed to find the fastest path to growth with limited resources.
tactics: Viral loops (every user action that invites another user)
Product-led growth (product itself is the marketing)
Reverse trials (give full access, then limit)
Integration partnerships that distribute you through another product's user base

concepts.name: Retention Loop Design
concepts.definition: Engineering your product so that continued use creates increasing value, making it progressively harder to leave.

loop_types.example: The more data I put in, the more personalised the output, the harder to leave
My colleagues/customers are in here — I can't leave without disrupting them
Daily use is built into my routine — I don't think about switching
I've built so much in here (history, templates, settings) that the switching cost is high

concepts.name: Upsell & Cross-Sell Architecture
concepts.definition: Systematically increasing revenue per customer through higher tiers and adjacent products.
cross_sell_principles: Recommend at moment of success, not at signup
Offer adjacent value, not just more of the same
Let behaviour data, not guesswork, drive recommendations

concepts.name: Referral Flywheel Design
concepts.definition: A systematic mechanism where existing customers reliably bring in new customers, compounding growth.
concepts.flywheel_law: The best referral programs make the referrer look good to their network, not just reward them financially.

concepts.name: Product-Market Fit Scoring
concepts.definition: Measuring how strongly your product satisfies a specific market's needs — the precondition for sustainable growth.
concepts.sean_ellis_test: Ask customers: 'How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?' If >40% answer 'Very disappointed', you likely have PMF.
signals_of_pmf: Users complain loudly when you change something
Customers use the product in ways you didn't anticipate
signals_of_missing_pmf: Users politely interested but not passionate
Growth requires constant heavy marketing spend

concepts.name: Profitability Levers
concepts.definition: The specific mechanisms available to any business to increase net profit.
